session_meta.research_objective:
Focus group guide exploring how men in the UK make everyday food
choices, how social context, work, hobbies, health, taste and other
people shape what they eat, how gender and masculinity may influence
food choices, and what would need to change for plant-based foods to
become more acceptable or appealing.
session_meta.topic_domain: Masculinity, food choice, animal product consumption, and plant-based eating
session_meta.participant_collective_identity: Men in the UK reflecting on food choices, male friendship, gender norms, and plant-based eating
session_meta.moderator_knowledge_brief:
Explore (1) everyday food decision-making, (2) the social contexts in
which men spend time with male friends, (3) the influence of other
people, work, hobbies, health, nutrition and taste on food choices,
(4) whether participants perceive gender as shaping what they eat,
(5) social acceptability and gendered meanings attached to vegetarian,
vegan, plant-based, feminine or masculine foods, and (6) what personal,
social and practical changes would make plant-based eating more viable
or appealing. The discussion should remain exploratory, non-judgmental,
and non-leading.

initial_session_plan.thematisation_approach: These participants will be framed as men reflecting on their own everyday lived experiences — the mundane, practical, social realities of how they eat and spend time with other men. The framing will stay grounded and concrete throughout, treating them as knowledgeable about their own lives rather than as representatives of a category or spokesmen for masculinity in the abstract.
priority_research_areas: Gender and food choice (Section 3): High risk of socially desirable, abstract, or defensive responses — 'I don't think gender affects me at all' delivered without any real behavioural grounding. Need careful behavioural anchoring and patience with deflection.

Plant-based shift and barriers (Section 4): Risk of convergence on practical/cost barriers as a socially safe explanation, masking identity-level or social-norm resistance. Need sharpening moves ready if consensus hardens too quickly.

Social acceptability of food choices and gendered meanings (implicit across Sections 3–5): Men may acknowledge norms at the level of 'other men' while distancing themselves personally. Need to track individual-vs.-group attributions carefully and probe personal behaviour specifically.

What would make plant-based more appealing (Section 5): Risk of abstract, prescriptive answers ('if it tasted better', 'if it was cheaper') rather than personally anchored insight. Behavioural grounding and redirecting to specific moments or people will matter.

known_risk_conditions: Topic may produce socially desirable or self-distancing answers on gender — 'I just eat what I want, gender doesn't come into it'. Use behavioural grounding (specific past moments, real decisions) to get below the surface claim.

Group may converge quickly on price, taste, or convenience as barriers to plant-based eating — these are cognitively available and socially safe. Plan a sharpening hypothetical: 'If it tasted identical and cost the same, what then?'

initial_session_plan.directivity_plan: Sections 0–1: Low directivity. Welcome, orient, let participants settle in. Light probes only where something genuinely rich surfaces — do not exhaust topics. Section 2: Moderate directivity. Begin grounding participants behaviourally in real food decisions before the gender question lands. Section 3: Higher directivity. This is where socially desirable abstraction is most likely — push for specific past moments, and be ready to gently surface tensions between stated views and described behaviours. Sections 4–5: Moderate-to-high directivity depending on what has emerged in Section 3. If identity resistance has been strong, push harder on specific conditions that would change behaviour. If group has been forthcoming, allow more peer-to-peer exchange and step back. Section 6: Minimal directivity — light closing invitation only.

time_budget.budget_rationale: Main topic sections (3, 4, 5) receive the largest combined share (~60%) as they carry the research. Context sections (1, 2) receive moderate allocation (~28%) — they warm the group up and generate behavioural baseline data that feeds later probing. Intro and closing are minimal (~12%) — enough to orient and close gracefully without eating into discussion time.

discussion_guide.scripted_question:
Hi everyone, thanks so much for joining the focus group today. We’re
going to take about 45 minutes to talk about your food choices and
opinions, and this will be recorded for research purposes. Try not to
overthink the questions, and simply speak freely. There are no right
or wrong answers. Please be respectful of your fellow focus group
members, and keep your responses relatively brief to allow time for
everyone to speak. But remember that this is a conversation, not an
interview, so you can jump in when you have something to say and you
don’t have to take turns answering each question, but you can if you
want to. Okay great, let’s start by going around and saying your name
and where in the UK you’re coming from today.

How do you decide what to eat?
suggested_probes: Do other people influence what you eat? If so, tell us more about how.
Do your work or hobbies influence what foods you eat? Tell us more about how.
How important is health and nutrition?

discussion_guide.scripted_question:
Do you think your gender influences what you eat? Tell us more about
why or why not.
suggested_probes: Is it socially acceptable for men to eat vegetarian or vegan foods?

discussion_guide.scripted_question:
Imagine you decided to go plant-based — what would need to change in
your life for you to do that?
suggested_probes: How would your family and friends react to this?
How might it change the way you shop or cook?

What might make plant-based foods more appealing to you or other men
you know?

Okay everyone, that’s our time. Thanks so much for participating
today. Before we finish, is there anything else you would like to add
about food choices, gender, masculinity, or plant-based eating?

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section was introductory, establishing participant geography and domestic context. A spontaneous thread emerged around commuter train unreliability — participants from the South East and East of England framing it not merely as inconvenience but as a structural constraint shaping employment choices, daily energy, and family life. The North West and South West participants partially dissented, noting car-based commutes insulate them from the worst of this, though they recognised the broader theme of transport limiting opportunity.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The priority here was simply getting all five participants introduced and present. Andrew, Daniel, and Paul moved quickly into an unplanned train reliability discussion; I let it run briefly to build rapport and group cohesion before redirecting to draw in the two silent participants. Direct address to John and Nick worked — both joined without resistance. The section closed cleanly with a pivot to the first substantive question. The early digression cost a little time but seemed to warm the group up usefully.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section centred on the conditions that enable regular third-place socialising — stability, proximity, habit, and deliberate commitment. A productive tension emerged between participants who have established local rhythms (John, Nick) and those who haven't (Andrew, Paul), with the group converging on a shared insight: regularity requires active decision-making, not passive waiting. Geography and commuter fatigue featured as structural barriers, but participants also interrogated their own agency in ways that felt genuinely self-critical rather than defensive.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The section opened with John and Andrew in a natural bilateral exchange; I held back and let it develop because the dynamic was productive and the theme substantive. I intervened once to draw in Paul and Daniel, then separately addressed Nick — direct address worked cleanly both times. The moderator summary at close was slightly long but served to name the effort-versus-habit tension explicitly before transitioning topics. Overall the section ran well with minimal steering needed.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section explored how commute-induced exhaustion erodes domestic planning capacity — meal planning as a proxy for broader loss of agency. A productive tension emerged between Daniel's structural argument (some things simply cannot coexist with chaos) and Andrew's self-critical counter (chaos becomes an excuse to stop trying). John reframed both with a third position: stop waiting for ideal conditions. Nick partially dissented, acknowledging the commute's outsized explanatory role and offering a calmer outside perspective.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: Daniel and Paul opened strongly without prompting; I let the exchange run until it risked looping, then drew in Andrew and John with a direct question anchored to Paul's unresolved tension. That worked well — Andrew's self-critical turn enriched the discussion considerably. I named the Andrew-Daniel disagreement explicitly to sharpen it for John and Nick, which produced John's reframe. Direct address to Nick was necessary and yielded a useful structural contrast. The closing summary and pivot to gender felt clean; transition timing was right.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section examined gendered domestic labour through the lens of meal planning, then pivoted into a sharper meta-debate: whether naming passivity constitutes genuine reflection or merely performs it. A productive tension emerged between John's scepticism of 'performed awareness' and Nick's defence of noticing as meaningful in itself, before Paul radicalised the critique — only for Daniel's concrete example (one weekly meal with his wife) to ground the abstraction and shift the group's emotional register toward cautious agency.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The gender prompt opened productively without heavy steering; I intervened mainly to surface the John-Nick tension for the wider group, then drew in Andrew, Daniel, and Paul when the exchange risked becoming bilateral. Direct address to Daniel at a moment when he'd been quiet yielded the section's most generative contribution. The transition to plant-based eating landed cleanly on the back of Daniel's example — the emotional groundwork of the passivity debate made the pivot feel earned rather than abrupt.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section deepened the passivity-versus-action tension from Section 3 into something more psychologically precise: the distinction between not trying and trying-then-failing, and what each demands you know about yourself. The group converged on a shared anxiety — that genuine effort makes comfortable self-narratives unavailable. Daniel's friction reframe shifted the register from willpower to persistence, and John's closing provocation complicated the whole thread: over-analysis may itself be a form of avoidance.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: Andrew and Daniel opened with enough momentum that I stayed back, intervening only to surface Andrew's failure-aversion insight for the group and route it to Paul, then Nick. Direct address to Nick was necessary and productive; connecting Paul's 'performance' language back to John was a deliberate callback that landed well. The closing pivot to plant-based appeal required some force — John's observation was a natural endpoint, so the transition risked feeling imposed, but framing it as a flip rather than a redirect helped.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section pushed the doing-versus-understanding tension to its most psychologically precise point: the distinction between not knowing and knowing-but-not-acting, and why the latter may be harder to bear. The group converged on a shared recognition that protective self-narratives — 'it wasn't for us,' 'the timing isn't right' — function as deliberate shields against uncomfortable truths. Andrew's live retreat from his own commitment dramatised the argument in real time, with Paul and Daniel together insisting that certainty is neither prerequisite nor guarantee.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: I held back for most of this section — the John-Nick exchange and the Andrew-Nick convergence needed room, and intervening would have flattened it. My two substantive moves were routing John's challenge back to Nick, then pulling in Andrew, Daniel, and Paul through targeted callbacks. Drawing Daniel in late was deliberate: his concrete experience grounded what had become increasingly abstract. The closing invitation for final additions served partly to decompress — the emotional intensity needed somewhere to exhale before the session ended.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section landed on mutuality as the condition underlying all earlier talk of commitment and agency: individual resolve is insufficient without relational alignment. John's intervention reframed the session's recurring doing-versus-waiting tension — some conditions genuinely must be right, and partnership is one of them. Andrew's closing admission that he had never asked his wife whether she wanted change collapsed the distinction between performed and genuine reflection, concretising what earlier sections had only approached theoretically.
